item.research_question: How does the change in deformation mechanism from crystallographic slip at room temperature to transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) at cryogenic temperatures impact the magnetic and electrical properties of the Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 high entropy alloy?
item.processing_route: Arc-melted from pure elements (>99.5 wt.%), homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, solution heat treated at 900 °C for 1 h followed by oil quenching; tensile deformation applied at 298 K (RT) and 77 K (LN) to ~22% plastic strain at a strain rate of ≈ 4 × 10–1 s−1
item.test_conditions: Magnetic measurements performed in a cryogenic physical property measurement system (2–350 K) with fields up to 9 T; resistivity measured via four-point method; EBSD and XRD used for phase and strain analysis
key_findings: Yield strength increased from ~150 MPa at RT to 340 MPa at LN (≈130% increase).
HCP phase fraction increased from 0% to 66% following 22.5% plastic strain at 77 K.
Magnetic moment dropped significantly for deformed specimens compared to undeformed (e.g., 0.4 emu/g at 0.05 T vs 1.8 emu/g at 9 T for undeformed at 2 K).
Coercive fields for deformed samples were ~60% larger than undeformed samples (108–78 gauss for undeformed).
Residual resistivity increased by ~10% for RT deformed and ~25% for LN deformed samples.
An abrupt increase in magnetization at 70 K for the undeformed sample was smeared out in deformed samples.
The system exhibits a ferrimagnetic ground state with coexisting antiferromagnetic phase, evidenced by non-saturating magnetization up to 9 T.
item.mechanism: The deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation and increased defect density (dislocations, stacking faults) enhance antiferromagnetic coupling between Mn/Cr and Fe/Co moments, leading to reduced bulk magnetization, smeared magnetic transitions, and increased coercivity due to domain wall pinning by defects and residual stresses.
item.limitations: The magnetic ordering temperatures were not established due to limitations in the experimental setup (Tc exceeding 350 K); defect densities were not quantified; directional dependence of magnetic properties exists due to large grain size (200–250 μm).
item.future_work: Further investigation is needed to quantify defect densities and their specific impact on magnetic ground states; the study suggests that structural phase and defect density must both be considered to define physical properties.
quotes: Plastic deformation was accommodated via crystallographic slip at room temperature while transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) has been observed in samples deformed at 77 K.

Relatively small magnetic moments along with non-saturating magnetic field dependencies suggest that the ground state in the considered material is ferrimagnetic ordering with coexisting antiferromagnetic phase.

The HCP phase fraction increased with additional loading as shown in Fig. 4. Throughout the multiple loading increments, the fraction of the HCP phase increased from 0, before loading, to 66% following 22.5% plastic strain.

Limitations: The magnetic ordering temperatures were not established due to limitations in the experimental setup (Tc exceeding 350 K); defect densities were not quantified; directional dependence of magnetic properties exists due to large grain size (200–250 μm)..
